title: The flower-sweeper's song
hook: Sunita, once despised, is honored by gods and people (Theragatha, Sunita)

segments.voice: Yesterday, peacocks cried and a white crane flew ahead of the storm. Your line was the rains came. Did you stay put for a breath when the day turned? Today, a man people didn't want to look at. Day eight hundred.

Two crowds, one at each end of a single poem. At the start, the Buddha walks into the city with a company of monks around him, and a man who hauls away withered flowers sets down his carrying pole. At the end, that same man sits with a company of gods around him. The path met Sunita a few weeks ago, on that street, hearing the two words that made him a monk: come, monk. Today we stay with the second half of his song: the night alone, the dawn, and who comes to bow.
screen: `TWO CROWDS IN ONE POEM.` → `WE MET HIM ON THE STREET.` → `TODAY, THE NIGHT AND THE DAWN.`

segments.voice: First, the night. After the street, Sunita goes into the forest alone and does what the Teacher told him, without slacking. His song walks through the night watch by watch. In the first watch, he says, he remembered his former lives. In the middle watch, his divine eye was made clear. In the last, he split apart the mass of darkness. Second, the dawn. As the night ends and the sun comes up, Indra and Brahma come to him and bow with joined palms. The man who once bowed to everyone is now the one bowed to. And they speak: homage to you, finest of men, whose taints are destroyed; you are worthy of offerings. Hold on to that last phrase. Offerings are what people bring, and this was a man who once lived on little to eat. Third, the mirror. When the Buddha sees him, the song says, Sunita is surrounded by a company of gods, the way the Buddha was surrounded by monks on the morning they met. The poem's shape turns all the way round. Fourth, the smile. The Buddha smiles and speaks a verse: by discipline, by the holy life, by restraint and taming oneself, by these one becomes a brahmin; this is the highest brahmin. In the world of the poem, brahmin names the priestly families, honored by birth. Here it names a way of living. And notice who smiles. Sunita doesn't gloat over the people who once looked past him. He just tells it in order: the flowers, the street, the night, the dawn.
screen: `THREE WATCHES OF THE NIGHT.` · `INDRA AND BRAHMA BOW AT DAWN.` · `NOW HE STANDS AMONG THE GODS.` · `THE BUDDHA SMILES: A BRAHMIN BY CONDUCT.` · then, large: `ONCE DESPISED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor one humble worker. Choose someone whose work happens before you arrive or after you leave: the person who unlocks the building, the night shift at the hospital, whoever picked the fruit in your kitchen. Picture the hours they keep, the dark before dawn. Then, in your mind, put your palms together, the way Indra and Brahma did at sunrise for Sunita. No speech needed. Just let them be someone worth bowing to. If a judgment rises, notice it, and come back to the breath. The bell holds the time.
The flower-sweeper's song. Sunita's verses: a man who cleared away withered flowers, bowed to by gods at dawn and called worthy of offerings. Today's word.
Your line: once despised. Today, when someone's work makes your day easier, think of the hours behind it, and thank them for one specific thing. Day eight hundred.

howItsDone: Theravada teachers often tell Sunita's story, and the Buddha's closing words to him, when they teach that what makes a person noble is conduct, not birth.

myth: Sunita's song walks through his night alone, watch by watch
first his former lives, then the divine eye made clear, then the darkness split apart.
the gods call Sunita worthy of offerings
homage to you, finest of men, they say; you are worthy of offerings.
Sunita's song ends with him scolding the people who despised him
it ends with the Buddha's smile and a verse: one becomes a brahmin by discipline and restraint.

fork.setup: you're Sunita. it's sunrise after a night alone in the forest, and Indra and Brahma stand before you with joined palms. what does the song say comes next?
options: you go back to town to show the people who mocked you.
the Buddha sees you among the gods, smiles, and speaks a verse.
you bow to the gods, as you always bowed to everyone.
fork.reveal: the Buddha sees him surrounded by gods, as the Buddha himself was surrounded by monks the day they met, and smiles: a brahmin is made by discipline and restraint.

original.note: Pali: dakkhineyya, worthy of offerings. What Indra and Brahma call Sunita at dawn.

trapdoor: what you thought: a song about a gardener.
what it means: Sunita, once despised, spends a night alone in the forest, and at dawn the gods bow to him and call him worthy of offerings.
what a scholar hears: the song opens with the Buddha surrounded by monks and closes with Sunita surrounded by gods; the Buddha's verse makes brahmin a matter of conduct.

notes: Thag 12.2 (vv. 620–631 as remembered) paraphrased throughout. Confirm: low family, poor, little food; work as a remover of withered flowers (pupphachaddaka); despised, bowing to many; sets down his carrying pole; the Buddha stops out of compassion; 'come, monk' (ehi bhikkhu); alone in the forest; freed as night ends; Indra and Brahma bow with joined palms; the Buddha smiles and says one becomes a brahmin by austerity/discipline, the holy life, restraint and self-taming.
'In the world of the poem, brahmin names the priestly families, honored by birth' is a general framing, kept soft; confirm it is fair and not ranking anyone.

Auditor (fresh review): day 773 'Sunita the flower-scavenger' already retold the first half of this same poem (low birth, the pole, 'come, monk', the brahmin verse) with a near-identical bins/cleaner practice and myths. Rewrote hook, teach, practice, carry, word and all games to take the second half instead: the three night watches (v. 627), Indra and Brahma's homage 'dakkhineyyo' (vv. 628–629), and the mirror of 'bhikkhusanghapurakkhatam' (v. 622) with 'devasanghapurakkhatam' (v. 630). Also cut 'gods of the old stories' (dismissive) and 'honored by people too' (the poem names only gods; 'worthy of offerings' carries the human side). Confirm verse numbers, the night-watch paraphrase and दक्खिणेय्य.
